claim: Current optical microscope objectives of low magnification have low numerical aperture.
source: Current optical microscope objectives of low magnification have low numerical aperture and therefore have too little depth resolution and discrimination to perform well in confocal and nonlinear microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the abstract and introduction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Low numerical aperture objectives have too little depth resolution and discrimination to perform well in confocal and nonlinear microscopy.
source: Current optical microscope objectives of low magnification have low numerical aperture and therefore have too little depth resolution and discrimination to perform well in confocal and nonlinear microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation and is supported by established understanding of optical microscopy principles.

claim: The Mesolens can image objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of only a few microns.
source: We have built an optical lens system for 3D imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of only a few microns instead of the tens of microns currently attained, allowing sub-cellular detail to be resolved throughout the volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and imaging data presented in the manuscript, including Table 1 and Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Current low-magnification objectives achieve depth resolution of tens of microns.
source: We have built an optical lens system for 3D imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of only a few microns instead of the tens of microns currently attained, allowing sub-cellular detail to be resolved throughout the volume.
evidence: This is supported by measurements in Table 1 showing a 5x/0.15 N.A. lens has Z FWHM of 51 µm in epi mode and 38 µm in confocal mode.

claim: The Mesolens allows sub-cellular detail to be resolved throughout the volume of large specimens.
source: We have built an optical lens system for 3D imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of only a few microns instead of the tens of microns currently attained, allowing sub-cellular detail to be resolved throughout the volume.
evidence: This is demonstrated by images in Figures 4 and 5 showing individual cell nuclei throughout mouse embryos.

claim: Optical sectioning does not work with available low-magnification objectives because of their low numerical aperture.
source: During experiments with laser scanning confocal microscopes in the mid-1980s, it became obvious that the optical sectioning, which is the main advantage of the confocal method, did not work with the available low-magnification objectives, because of their low numerical aperture (N.A.) (White et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to White et al., 1987 and is consistent with established optical principles.

claim: In mouse embryos at the 10-12.5 day stage, major organs are developing.
source: In specimens such as mouse embryos at the 10–12.5 day stage, when the major organs are developing (Kaufman, 1992), it was impossible to see individual cells in the interior despite the lateral (XY) resolution being sufficient.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaufman, 1992, a reference work on mouse embryo development.

claim: With previous low-magnification objectives, it was impossible to see individual cells in the interior of mouse embryos despite sufficient lateral resolution.
source: In specimens such as mouse embryos at the 10–12.5 day stage, when the major organs are developing (Kaufman, 1992), it was impossible to see individual cells in the interior despite the lateral (XY) resolution being sufficient.
evidence: This is based on historical observations and is contrasted with the Mesolens performance shown in the data.

claim: Stitching and tiling of large datasets results in a checker board pattern in the final image due to inhomogeneity of illumination and focus height errors.
source: Since then, stitching and tiling of large datasets has proved to be possible using computer-controlled specimen stages, but this results in a checker board pattern in the final image due to inhomogeneity of illumination and focus height errors which often cannot be corrected by software.
evidence: This is stated as a known problem with stitching methods and is supported by a citation to Legesse et al., 2015.

claim: Commercial and open source software algorithms are available to perform stitching and tiling but inhomogeneities and problems with dataset registration are clearly visible.
source: Commercial and open source software algorithms are available to perform stitching and tiling but inhomogeneities and problems with dataset registration are clearly visible (Legesse et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Legesse et al., 2015.

claim: The Mesolens uses a continuous scanning laser spot that does not produce differences in fluorescence signal from one region of the image to another unless present in the specimen.
source: Because of the continuous scanning laser spot that we use with the Mesolens, we do not observe differences in fluorescence signal from one region of the image to another unless it is present in the specimen.
evidence: This is based on the design and operation of the Mesolens system as described by the authors.

claim: Methods to expand tissue volume using synthetic polymers have been demonstrated.
source: More recently, methods to expand the tissue volume using synthetic polymers have been demonstrated, increasing the size of the sub-micron sized structures until they can be imaged by an ordinary low-magnification, low-resolution lens, but this inevitably results in some tissue distortion (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Tissue expansion methods inevitably result in some tissue distortion.
source: More recently, methods to expand the tissue volume using synthetic polymers have been demonstrated, increasing the size of the sub-micron sized structures until they can be imaged by an ordinary low-magnification, low-resolution lens, but this inevitably results in some tissue distortion (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of expansion microscopy and is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: A 4x magnification lens with an N.A. of approximately 0.5 is needed to support imaging with sub-cellular resolution through entire specimens.
source: We decided that what was needed was a 4x magnification lens with an N.A. of approximately 0.5, rather than the 0.1 or 0.2 currently available, to support imaging with sub-cellular resolution through the entire specimen.
evidence: This is based on the authors' reasoning from optical principles (Equations 1 and 2) and design goals.

claim: Currently available low-magnification lenses have N.A. of 0.1 or 0.2.
source: We decided that what was needed was a 4x magnification lens with an N.A. of approximately 0.5, rather than the 0.1 or 0.2 currently available, to support imaging with sub-cellular resolution through the entire specimen.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of available lenses.

claim: Off-the-shelf camera lenses adapted for microscopy were found to be unsuitable because of poor aberration correction including high field curvature.
source: Off-the-shelf lenses with the right characteristics, for example camera lenses, which could be adapted for microscopy by placing the specimen in the plane intended for the camera sensor and forming a x4 image in what would normally be the object space, were found to be unsuitable because of poor aberration correction including high field curvature, particularly when focused deeply into specimens immersed in fluid.
evidence: This is based on the authors' testing and evaluation of alternative approaches.

claim: Zheng, Ou and Yang used a high-quality Pentax TV lens with an N.A. of approximately 0.3 to produce an image of a 10 mm diameter field with a lateral resolution of 1.56 µm.
source: The most successful attempt with a camera lens has been made recently by Zheng, Ou and Yang (Zheng et al., 2013a; Ou et al., 2016) who used a high-quality Pentax TV lens with an N.A. of approximately 0.3 to produce an image of a 10 mm diameter field with a lateral resolution of 1.56 µm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2013a and Ou et al., 2016.

claim: For samples such as a 10 day old mouse embryo, which is 2-3 mm thick, an immersion lens is needed for optically-sectioned imaging.
source: For samples such as a 10 day old mouse embryo, which is 2–3 mm thick, however, an immersion lens is needed for optically-sectioned imaging, so that the spherical aberration introduced when imaging from air and through thicker material than the thin coverslip for which the lens is designed does not destroy the optical performance as the light is focused into the specimen.
evidence: This is based on established optical principles regarding spherical aberration.

claim: A 10 day old mouse embryo is 2-3 mm thick.
source: For samples such as a 10 day old mouse embryo, which is 2–3 mm thick, however, an immersion lens is needed for optically-sectioned imaging, so that the spherical aberration introduced when imaging from air and through thicker material than the thin coverslip for which the lens is designed does not destroy the optical performance as the light is focused into the specimen.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of mouse embryo specimens.

claim: Large-field of view water-immersion lenses have been developed for photolithography in semiconductor device manufacture.
source: Large-field of view (FOV) water-immersion lenses of great complexity have been developed for photolithography in the manufacture of semiconductor devices, but these work only with monochromatic light (e.g. at a wavelength of 193 nm) and a fixed object distance so they are not useful for biomedical imaging (Matsuyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsuyama et al., 2006.

claim: Photolithography lenses work only with monochromatic light and a fixed object distance so they are not useful for biomedical imaging.
source: Large-field of view (FOV) water-immersion lenses of great complexity have been developed for photolithography in the manufacture of semiconductor devices, but these work only with monochromatic light (e.g. at a wavelength of 193 nm) and a fixed object distance so they are not useful for biomedical imaging (Matsuyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on the known specifications of photolithography lenses and the requirements of biomedical imaging.

claim: Fourier Ptychographic Microscopy (FPM) can give a very wide field of view image with sub-micron resolution.
source: Fourier Ptychographic Microscopy (FPM) can give a very wide field of view image with sub-micron resolution (Zheng et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2013b.

claim: FPM has a depth of focus of approximately 0.3 mm.
source: However, the depth of focus is purposefully large (~0.3 mm) in order to provide a large tolerance to microscope slide placement errors.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of FPM based on the cited literature.

claim: FPM's large depth of focus is not suited to confocal laser scanning microscopy, where a small depth of focus is needed for optical sectioning.
source: This very large depth of focus is not suited to confocal laser scanning microscopy, where a small depth of focus is needed for optical sectioning of the imaged specimen.
evidence: This is based on established principles of confocal microscopy.

claim: The low N.A. lens used in wide-field FPM is for use in air only.
source: Also, the low N.A. lens used in wide-field FPM is for use in air only.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of FPM based on the cited literature.

claim: Air immersion gives dramatic fall-off in axial resolution performance at depth when imaging thick tissues because of spherical aberration.
source: While this is acceptable for thin tissue sections, restriction to air immersion would give dramatic fall-off in axial resolution performance at depth when imaging thick tissues because of spherical aberration, for which there are presently no correction collars or any other means of compensation.
evidence: This is based on established optical principles regarding spherical aberration.

claim: The current FPM method is not a fluorescence technique.
source: Furthermore, as noted by Zheng et al. the current FPM method is not a fluorescence technique.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Zheng et al.'s work.

claim: FPM is not suitable for fluorescence imaging of either thin or thick specimens in either 2D or 3D.
source: Therefore, while FPM gives high-resolution color images of thin specimens such as pathology slides, it is not suitable for fluorescence imaging of either thin or thick specimens in either 2D or 3D.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of FPM described in the text and cited literature.

claim: Fluorescence Talbot microscopy can provide imaging over a large field of view.
source: Fluorescence Talbot microscopy is another method that can provide imaging over a large field of view.
evidence: This is stated as a known capability of the technique.

claim: Fluorescence Talbot microscopy usually involves placing the specimen in direct contact with the imaging sensor.
source: This usually involves placing the specimen in direct contact with the imaging sensor (Pang et al., 2013), which, because of the requirement for immersion and mounting of specimens in high-index material, is impractical for thick tissue imaging.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pang et al., 2013.

claim: Pang et al. overcame the limitation of requiring specimen-sensor contact in Talbot microscopy.
source: The work of Pang et al. overcomes this limitation (Pang et al., 2013), and makes possible imaging of specimens spatially separated from the sensor with fluorescence contrast and an exceptionally wide field of view.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pang et al., 2013.

claim: The reported depth of focus limit of 60 µm for Talbot microscopy is too large to be useful for optically sectioning of thick tissue volumes.
source: However, while the lateral performance is good the reported depth of focus limit of 60 µm is too large to be useful for optically sectioning of thick tissue volumes.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the requirements for optical sectioning and the cited performance of Talbot microscopy.

claim: The imaging speed of 23 s of the Talbot microscopy instrument described by Pang et al. is attractive.
source: The imaging speed of 23 s of the instrument described by Pang et al. is attractive but the reported unevenness of Talbot spots over an area of 1 mm x 1 mm of 4.73% is very high when compared with both standard wide-field imaging and our wide-field imaging using the Mesolens.
evidence: This is based on the cited performance specifications from Pang et al.

claim: The reported unevenness of Talbot spots over an area of 1 mm x 1 mm of 4.73% is very high when compared with standard wide-field imaging and Mesolens imaging.
source: The imaging speed of 23 s of the instrument described by Pang et al. is attractive but the reported unevenness of Talbot spots over an area of 1 mm x 1 mm of 4.73% is very high when compared with both standard wide-field imaging and our wide-field imaging using the Mesolens.
evidence: This is based on comparison of cited performance data with the authors' observations.

claim: Tsai et al. performed large FOV two-photon microscopy using a commercial low-magnification objective lens (XL Fluor 4X/340, N.A.=0.28, Olympus).
source: Tsai et al. have performed large FOV two-photon microscopy using a commercial low-magnification objective lens (XL Fluor 4X/340, N.A.=0.28, Olympus), but they observe modest depth penetration and low axial resolution of 16 µm, as expected from the N.A. of the objective (Tsai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2015.

claim: Tsai et al. observed modest depth penetration and low axial resolution of 16 µm.
source: Tsai et al. have performed large FOV two-photon microscopy using a commercial low-magnification objective lens (XL Fluor 4X/340, N.A.=0.28, Olympus), but they observe modest depth penetration and low axial resolution of 16 µm, as expected from the N.A. of the objective (Tsai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2015.

claim: For objectives designed for multi-photon imaging, the performance at visible wavelengths is poor or unpublished.
source: Furthermore, for objectives designed for multi-photon imaging, the performance (primarily colour correction) at visible wavelengths is poor or unpublished.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of multi-photon objectives.

claim: Serial two-photon tomography can provide very high lateral resolution images of the fluorescent mouse brain.
source: Serial two-photon tomography can provide very high lateral resolution images of the fluorescent mouse brain (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oh et al., 2014.

claim: Serial two-photon tomography requires the tissue to be destroyed because of microtome sectioning, making repeat imaging impossible.
source: However, this imaging method requires the tissue to be destroyed because of the microtome sectioning needed and this makes repeat imaging impossible.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of serial two-photon tomography based on the cited literature.

claim: Serial two-photon tomography requires stitching and tiling of multiple datasets because of the large diameter of the tissue.
source: More importantly, stitching and tiling of multiple datasets is required because of the large diameter of the tissue, and this can result in poor image registration and differences in fluorescence signal from one dataset to another.
evidence: This is inferred from the known characteristics of serial two-photon tomography and the cited literature.

claim: Some commercial microscopes are described as capable of imaging the same specimen from the macro-scale to the micro-scale.
source: We finally note that some commercial microscopes are described as capable of imaging the same specimen from the macro-scale to the micro-scale (e.g. AZ100 Multizoom, Nikon) but at the low magnifications that permit imaging of large specimens, the N.A. of these microscopes is low, and thus the performance is as for a low N.A. objective.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of commercial microscopes.

claim: At low magnifications that permit imaging of large specimens, the N.A. of commercial multizoom microscopes is low.
source: We finally note that some commercial microscopes are described as capable of imaging the same specimen from the macro-scale to the micro-scale (e.g. AZ100 Multizoom, Nikon) but at the low magnifications that permit imaging of large specimens, the N.A. of these microscopes is low, and thus the performance is as for a low N.A. objective.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of commercial microscopes.

claim: The lens was developed from first principles with the aid of optical design software (Zemax).
source: The lens was developed from first principles with the aid of optical design software (Zemax), and optimizing for an imaging FOV of 6 mm and an N.A. as close as possible to 0.5.
evidence: This describes the design methodology used by the authors.

claim: The FOV was chosen to match the diameter of a 12.5 day old mouse embryo specimen.
source: The FOV was chosen to match the diameter of a 12.5 day old mouse embryo specimen, and the value of N.A. was chosen based on the well-known equations (Pawley, 2006)
evidence: This describes the design rationale based on the intended application.

claim: The value of N.A. was chosen based on well-known equations relating resolution to numerical aperture.
source: The FOV was chosen to match the diameter of a 12.5 day old mouse embryo specimen, and the value of N.A. was chosen based on the well-known equations (Pawley, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pawley, 2006 and the equations presented.

claim: The depth of field (z resolution) is inversely proportional to the square of the numerical aperture.
source: Since the depth of field (z resolution) is inversely proportional to the square of the numerical aperture, it rapidly becomes poor for low N.A. lenses.
evidence: This is based on Equation 2 and established optical principles.

claim: Below N.A.=0.45 the lateral resolution remains tolerable but the axial resolution is no longer sufficient for resolving sub-cellular details.
source: Below N.A.=0.45 the lateral resolution remains tolerable but the axial resolution is no longer sufficient for resolving sub-cellular details (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The large working distance was required to enable focusing through the embryo which, at 10 days old, is around 3 mm thick.
source: Another important design parameter was the large working distance, to enable focusing through the embryo which, at 10 days old, is around 3 mm thick.
evidence: This describes a design requirement based on the specimen characteristics.

claim: The large working distance dictated that the lens elements should be physically large to accommodate wide collection angles for light originating at a large distance from the lens.
source: This dictated that the lens elements should be physically large, to accommodate the wide collection angles for light originating at a large distance from the lens.
evidence: This is based on optical design principles and geometric considerations.

claim: Embryos may be examined in a variety of optically dissimilar fluids such as water, glycerol, oil and benzyl benzoate.
source: Because embryos may be examined in a variety of optically dissimilar fluids such as water, glycerol, oil and benzyl benzoate (such as for the clearing liquid BABB), it was necessary to make the lens suitable for use with different immersion fluids and mounting media.
evidence: This is stated as a known requirement for embryo imaging.

claim: The Mesolens was designed for immersion into non-corrosive immersion media such as oil (Type DF), water and glycerol.
source: The Mesolens was designed for immersion into non-corrosive immersion media such as oil (Type DF), water and glycerol.
evidence: This describes a design specification of the Mesolens.

claim: BABB is used only as a mounting medium, and the specimen and BABB are separated from the immersion fluid by a type 1.5 coverslip.
source: We use BABB only as a mounting medium, and the specimen and BABB are separated from the immersion fluid by a type 1.5 coverslip.
evidence: This describes the protocol used with the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens has two knurled rings on the lens barrel to shift lens element groups for correction of spherical and other aberrations for different liquids.
source: This meant providing means to shift lens element groups during use so that adequate correction for spherical and other aberrations could be obtained for the different liquids. In practice, the necessary shift was controlled by two knurled rings on the lens barrel, similarly to a standard microscope objective that corrects for the coverslip thickness or immersion fluid.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the Mesolens.

claim: A further interchangeable flat compensator plate was incorporated into the design to compensate for spherical aberrations introduced by different immersion fluids.
source: In addition, a further interchangeable flat compensator plate was incorporated into the design to compensate for spherical aberrations introduced by the different immersion fluids, with a thickness specific to the immersion medium used.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the Mesolens.

claim: The main challenge in the lens design was to achieve colour correction between 400 nm and 700 nm.
source: The main challenge in our lens design was to achieve the colour correction between 400 nm and 700 nm (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a design challenge and is supported by spot diagrams in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All glass types used in the Mesolens had to be tested for auto-fluorescence.
source: Also, the diverse glass types required all had to be tested for auto-fluorescence, and the precise refractive index of each selected sample had to be ascertained and the lens design adjusted to accommodate the small variations from one melt to another of nominally the same glass.
evidence: This describes a quality control step in the lens fabrication.

claim: The Mesolens comprises 15 optical elements of up to 63 mm in diameter when used in laser scanning confocal mode.
source: In total the Mesolens comprises of 15 optical elements of up to 63 mm in diameter when used in laser scanning confocal mode.
evidence: This describes the physical construction of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens comprises 17 elements for wide-field epi-fluorescence mode.
source: This increases to 17 elements for wide-field epi-fluorescence mode, where a (removable) chromatic reflector with a 30 degree angle of incidence with a custom mercury-line coating designed specifically for this angle of incidence (Chroma Technology Corp.) was incorporated into the optical train to introduce the incoherent light source, as shown in the insert to Figure 1.
evidence: This describes the configuration for wide-field mode and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A tilted compensating plate was added to eliminate astigmatism introduced by the chromatic reflector.
source: A tilted compensating plate, similar to the chromatic reflector but anti-reflection coated only, was added to eliminate astigmatism introduced by the chromatic reflector (Chroma Technology Corp.).
evidence: This describes a design feature to correct for aberrations.

claim: The lens design required manufacture and mounting of the optical elements to fine tolerances, e.g. centration to better than 3 µm.
source: The lens design required manufacture and mounting of the optical elements to fine tolerances, e.g. centration to better than 3 µm.
evidence: This describes the manufacturing specifications.

claim: The Mesolens cannot be fitted into an ordinary microscope frame.
source: With elements of up to 63 mm in diameter and a scan lens with an aperture diameter of 30 mm the Mesolens cannot be fitted into an ordinary microscope frame and when used in scanned image modes such as confocal, the scanning mirrors have to be very large.
evidence: This is inferred from the physical dimensions of the Mesolens components.

claim: When used in scanned image modes such as confocal, the scanning mirrors have to be very large.
source: With elements of up to 63 mm in diameter and a scan lens with an aperture diameter of 30 mm the Mesolens cannot be fitted into an ordinary microscope frame and when used in scanned image modes such as confocal, the scanning mirrors have to be very large.
evidence: This is inferred from the optical requirements of the Mesolens system.

claim: Custom mirrors made from lightweight beryllium and back-thinned to reduce mass were used with a galvo scanner (8360K, Cambridge Technology).
source: We used custom mirrors together with a galvo scanner (8360K, Cambridge Technology) which were made from lightweight beryllium and back-thinned to reduce the mass.
evidence: This describes the scanning system components.

claim: The scanning mirrors were required to be flat to λ/10 for sufficiently small aberrations.
source: These mirrors were required to be flat to λ/10 for sufficiently small aberrations.
evidence: This describes a specification for the scanning mirrors.

claim: A multi-element scan lens made by Beck Optronic Solutions was used to image the back focal plane of the Mesolens into an aperture of 30 mm diameter.
source: A multi-element scan lens made to our design by Beck Optronic Solutions was used to image the back focal plane of the Mesolens into an aperture of 30 mm diameter.
evidence: This describes a component of the optical system.

claim: The scan lens consisted of 6 optical elements and was corrected for astigmatism, spherical aberration and chromatic aberrations for wavelengths between 400 nm and 750 nm.
source: The scan lens consisted of 6 optical elements, and was corrected for astigmatism, spherical aberration and chromatic aberrations for wavelengths between 400 nm and 750 nm.
evidence: This describes the specifications of the scan lens.

claim: An upright microscope (Optiphot, Nikon) was modified by removing all but the stage, substage condenser, illuminator and base.
source: We sawed through an upright microscope (Optiphot, Nikon) to remove all but the stage, substage condenser, illuminator and base.
evidence: This describes the construction of the microscope system.

claim: A computer-controlled z-positioning system (Optiscan II, Prior Scientific) was added to the modified microscope.
source: We positioned this underneath the Mesolens and added a computer-controlled z-positioning system (Optiscan II, Prior Scientific).
evidence: This describes a component of the microscope system.

claim: The condenser lens was of smaller aperture than the Mesolens and could not fill the field of the Mesolens.
source: The condenser lens was of smaller aperture than the Mesolens and although it had a high-enough N.A. it could not fill the field of the Mesolens: for this, a new type of condenser would have to be designed.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current system.

claim: With a 6 mm FOV the number of pixels required for full Nyquist sampling of the image with the design lateral resolution of 0.6 µm is 20000 x 20000 pixels.
source: We note that with a 6 mm FOV the number of pixels required for a full Nyquist sampling of the image with the design lateral resolution of 0.6 µm is 20000 x 20000 pixels.
evidence: This is calculated from the FOV and resolution specifications.

claim: Using a minimum practical pixel dwell time of ca. 0.5 µs leads to an acquisition time of 200 s for a full FOV, full resolution image.
source: Using a minimum practical pixel dwell time of ca. 0.5 µs this leads to an acquisition time of 200 s for a full FOV, full resolution image.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of pixels and dwell time.

claim: The acquisition time for the Mesolens is similar to the time needed to image 6 mm x 6 mm using multiple images from a 10x objective with N.A.=0.4 and stitching them.
source: This is similar to the time needed to image 6 mm x 6 mm using multiple images from a 10x objective with N.A.=0.4 yielding a similar z-resolution, and stitching and tiling them.
evidence: This is based on comparison of acquisition times for different imaging approaches.

claim: With the Mesolens, problems of image alignment from stitching are circumvented.
source: With our imaging system, however, we circumvent the problems of image alignment.
evidence: This is inferred from the single-field imaging capability of the Mesolens.

claim: For full FOV imaging, the mirror speed is 92 Hz, which is at the limit of what such large mirrors can achieve.
source: In this case the mirror speed is a mere 92 Hz, which is at the limit of what such large mirrors can achieve.
evidence: This is based on the calculated scan parameters and physical limitations of the mirrors.

claim: The Mesolens imaging system is not slower in data rate than a standard laser scanning confocal microscope.
source: In summary, despite appearance, this imaging system is not slower in data rate than a standard laser scanning confocal microscope.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of acquisition times and data rates.

claim: For imaging in wide-field camera mode, full Nyquist sampling would require a camera with 400 megapixels.
source: For imaging in wide-field camera mode, full Nyquist sampling would require a camera with 400 megapixels.
evidence: This is calculated from the FOV and resolution specifications.

claim: The Mesolens has a magnification of intermediate image of 4x.
source: To summarize, the lens specifications were a magnification of intermediate image of 4x, an N.A. of 0.47, with a working distance of 3.15 mm, 3.40 mm, and 3.74 mm for water, glycerol, and oil immersion media respectively.
evidence: This is a stated specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens has an N.A. of 0.47.
source: To summarize, the lens specifications were a magnification of intermediate image of 4x, an N.A. of 0.47, with a working distance of 3.15 mm, 3.40 mm, and 3.74 mm for water, glycerol, and oil immersion media respectively.
evidence: This is a stated specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens has a working distance of 3.15 mm for water immersion.
source: To summarize, the lens specifications were a magnification of intermediate image of 4x, an N.A. of 0.47, with a working distance of 3.15 mm, 3.40 mm, and 3.74 mm for water, glycerol, and oil immersion media respectively.
evidence: This is a stated specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens has a working distance of 3.40 mm for glycerol immersion.
source: To summarize, the lens specifications were a magnification of intermediate image of 4x, an N.A. of 0.47, with a working distance of 3.15 mm, 3.40 mm, and 3.74 mm for water, glycerol, and oil immersion media respectively.
evidence: This is a stated specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens has a working distance of 3.74 mm for oil immersion.
source: To summarize, the lens specifications were a magnification of intermediate image of 4x, an N.A. of 0.47, with a working distance of 3.15 mm, 3.40 mm, and 3.74 mm for water, glycerol, and oil immersion media respectively.
evidence: This is a stated specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The distortion of the Mesolens was designed to be <0.7% at the periphery of the field.
source: The distortion was designed to be <0.7% at the periphery of the field.
evidence: This is a stated design specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens was colour-corrected over the full visible range to allow imaging of samples with multiple fluorescent labels.
source: The lens was colour-corrected over the full visible range to allow imaging of samples with multiple fluorescent labels.
evidence: This is a stated design specification of the Mesolens.

claim: The flatness of field was designed to be <3 µm for wavelengths of 400-700 nm across the 6 mm FOV.
source: The flatness of field was designed to be <3 µm for wavelengths of 400–700 nm across the 6 mm FOV.
evidence: This is a stated design specification of the Mesolens.

claim: A special test target was prepared by electron beam lithography of a 75 nm thick nickel-chromium coating on glass.
source: For quantitative measurements of resolution, a special test target was prepared by electron beam lithography of a 75 nm thick nickel-chromium coating on glass (Oldenbourg et al., 1993).
evidence: This describes the method for preparing the resolution test target and is supported by a citation.

claim: The lateral image resolution was judged by the visibility of a series of gratings with periods of 2 µm, 1 µm, and 0.5 µm.
source: The lateral image resolution was judged by the visibility of a series of gratings with periods of 2 µm, 1 µm, and 0.5 µm.
evidence: This describes the method for measuring resolution.

claim: In brightfield transmission mode and laser scanning confocal reflection mode, the resolution was found to be better than 1 µm.
source: In brightfield transmission mode using wide-field camera detection and in laser scanning confocal reflection mode using the 514 nm laser with photomultiplier tube (PMT) detection, the resolution was found to be better than 1 µm (Figure 2), with the 0.5 µm grating unresolved but the 1 µm grating clearly resolved.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 0.5 µm grating was unresolved but the 1 µm grating was clearly resolved.
source: In brightfield transmission mode using wide-field camera detection and in laser scanning confocal reflection mode using the 514 nm laser with photomultiplier tube (PMT) detection, the resolution was found to be better than 1 µm (Figure 2), with the 0.5 µm grating unresolved but the 1 µm grating clearly resolved.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Yellow/green-emitting fluorescent beads were used to evaluate the full point-spread function (PSF).
source: To evaluate the full point-spread function (PSF) we used yellow/green-emitting fluorescent beads.
evidence: This describes the method for PSF measurement.

claim: Similar PSF measurements were conducted with a conventional dry objective lens of similar magnification (5x/0.15 N.A HCX PL Fluotar, Leica Microsystems) for comparison.
source: For comparison similar measurements were conducted with a conventional dry objective lens of similar magnification (5x/0.15 N.A HCX PL Fluotar, Leica Microsystems) mounted on an upright microscope.
evidence: This describes the comparison method used.

claim: The measured XY FWHM for the Mesolens in epi mode is 0.7 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1.

claim: The measured Z FWHM for the Mesolens in epi mode is 7 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1.

claim: The measured XY FWHM for the Mesolens in confocal mode is 0.8 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1.

claim: The measured Z FWHM for the Mesolens in confocal mode is 8 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1.

claim: The theoretical XY FWHM for the Mesolens in epi mode is 0.6 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1 and calculated from optical theory.

claim: The theoretical Z FWHM for the Mesolens in epi mode is 6.3 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1 and calculated from optical theory.

claim: The theoretical XY FWHM for the Mesolens in confocal mode is 0.6 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1 and calculated from optical theory.

claim: The theoretical Z FWHM for the Mesolens in confocal mode is 3.7 µm.
source: Table 1. Measured and calculated values (µm) for the FWHM of the PSF in laser scanning confocal mode and wide-field epi-fluorescence mode for a conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. lens and the 4x/0.47 N.A. Mesolens used with oil immersion.
evidence: This is presented in Table 1 and calculated from optical theory.

claim: The lower than theoretical diffraction-limited resolution in z for laser scanning confocal mode was likely due to residual aberrations from the scan lens or from inaccuracies in the scan-lens-to-Mesolens separation.
source: The lower than theoretical diffraction-limited resolution in z for laser scanning confocal mode was likely due to residual (primarily astigmatic) aberrations from the scan lens or from inaccuracies in the scan-lens-to-Mesolens separation.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the measured performance.

claim: The astigmatic error was visible at the edges of the FOV.
source: The astigmatic error was visible at the edges of the FOV.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: The z resolution is sufficient to resolve sub-cellular detail and far superior to a standard objective lens with comparable magnification.
source: Nevertheless, the z resolution is, as we will demonstrate below, sufficient to resolve sub-cellular detail, and far superior to a standard objective lens with comparable magnification.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data in Table 1 and images in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The z-resolution in wide-field epi-fluorescence mode is 7 µm, which is only somewhat higher than the theoretical resolution (6.3 µm).
source: The results are presented in Table 1 and shows that the z-resolution is 7 µm, which is only somewhat higher than the theoretical resolution (6.3 µm) and there are some residual astigmatic aberrations.
evidence: This is based on the measurements presented in Table 1.

claim: The lack of improvement of the axial resolution in laser scanning confocal mode is likely due to aberrations in the scan lens and illumination system.
source: The lack of improvement of the axial resolution in laser scanning confocal mode is therefore likely due to aberrations in the scan lens and illumination system.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on comparison of confocal and wide-field performance.

claim: The laser scanning confocal mode still achieves optical sectioning not present with wide-field epi-fluorescence mode.
source: Nevertheless, the laser scanning confocal mode still achieves optical sectioning not present with wide-field epi-fluorescence mode.
evidence: This is based on the known principles of confocal microscopy and the imaging data.

claim: The flatness of field was measured to be <=3 µm over the central 4.2 mm of the FOV.
source: The flatness of field was measured to be <=3 µm over the central 4.2 mm of the FOV in reasonable agreement with the design specifications.
evidence: This is a measured performance characteristic.

claim: A light-emitting diode (HLMP-2855, Broadcom) was used as a specimen of standard luminosity to measure relative optical throughput efficiency.
source: In order to make measurements of the relative optical throughput efficiency of the Mesolens as compared with a commercial low-magnification, low numerical aperture lens (4x/0.1 N.A. Plan, Nikon) a light-emitting diode (HLMP-2855, Broadcom) was used as a specimen of standard luminosity (Beach and Duling, 1993).
evidence: This describes the method for measuring optical throughput and is supported by a citation.

claim: Using the same exposure time the intensity with the Mesolens was found to be 25x that with the conventional 4x/0.1 N.A. objective.
source: Using the same exposure time the intensity with the Mesolens was found to be 25x that with the conventional objective, in good agreement with the 4.7 times higher N.A. available from the Mesolens.
evidence: This is a measured result from the throughput comparison.

claim: The 25x higher intensity is in good agreement with the 4.7 times higher N.A. available from the Mesolens.
source: Using the same exposure time the intensity with the Mesolens was found to be 25x that with the conventional objective, in good agreement with the 4.7 times higher N.A. available from the Mesolens.
evidence: This is based on the relationship between N.A. and light collection efficiency.

claim: The on-axis transmission of the Mesolens system at 488 nm is 11%.
source: To measure the optical throughput we compared the laser power immediately after the beam splitter in the periscope (see Figure 1) with the laser power at the specimen plane at a wavelength of 488 nm, and we measured an on-axis transmission of 11%.
evidence: This is a measured result.

claim: A significant loss in optical throughput results from overfilling the top mirror in the periscope, which is required to achieve the flattest possible wavefront.
source: A significant loss results from overfilling the top mirror in the periscope, which is required in order to achieve the flattest possible wavefront.
evidence: This is the authors' explanation for part of the optical loss.

claim: There are additional losses from the scanning mirrors and in the scan lens.
source: There are also additional losses from the scanning mirrors and in the scan lens.
evidence: This is stated as a source of optical loss in the system.

claim: The optical throughput of a standard microscope objective can be several tens of percent.
source: Although the optical throughput of a standard microscope objective can be several tens of percent, the transmission of the complete system is more similar to what we measure here.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of standard objectives.

claim: The transmission of the complete microscope system is more similar to the Mesolens system transmission than the objective alone.
source: Although the optical throughput of a standard microscope objective can be several tens of percent, the transmission of the complete system is more similar to what we measure here.
evidence: This is based on the authors' comparison with commercial systems.

claim: The transmission value of the complete system is rarely given explicitly by microscope manufacturers.
source: We also note that the transmission value of the complete system is rarely given explicitly by microscope manufacturers but, based on the quoted power of the laser system (e.g. 50 mW for a Krypton-Argon laser operating at a wavelength of 488 nm) and measuring the maximum average power at the specimen plane (e.g. 3 mW after the objective lens), we measure a similar magnitude of optical loss with commercial confocal microscopes compared to the Mesolens.
evidence: This is based on the authors' observations of commercial systems.

claim: Based on measurements, commercial confocal microscopes have a similar magnitude of optical loss compared to the Mesolens.
source: We also note that the transmission value of the complete system is rarely given explicitly by microscope manufacturers but, based on the quoted power of the laser system (e.g. 50 mW for a Krypton-Argon laser operating at a wavelength of 488 nm) and measuring the maximum average power at the specimen plane (e.g. 3 mW after the objective lens), we measure a similar magnitude of optical loss with commercial confocal microscopes compared to the Mesolens.
evidence: This is based on the authors' measurements of commercial systems.

claim: The good transmission of the Mesolens itself is confirmed by comparison with a 4x/0.1 N.A. lens in camera mode.
source: The good transmission of the Mesolens itself is also confirmed by our comparison of the transmission of the Mesolens with that of a 4x/0.1 N.A. lens in camera mode.
evidence: This is based on the throughput comparison measurements described earlier.

claim: Figure 3 shows wide-field epi-fluorescence data from an explant culture of rat embryonic brain as a colour merge of three camera images at the same focus position.
source: Figure 3 and the Video 1 show wide-field epi-fluorescence data from an explant culture of rat embryonic brain as a colour merge of three camera images at the same focus position.
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 3.

claim: In the rat brain preparation, blue fluorescence is of nuclei stained for DNA with DAPI.
source: In this preparation, the blue fluorescence is of nuclei stained for DNA with DAPI, neurones show green because of Alexa 488 conjugated to an antibody against beta-III tubulin and astrocytes are red because of Alexa 546 conjugated to anti-GFAP (glial fibrillary acid protein).
evidence: This describes the staining protocol used.

claim: In the rat brain preparation, neurons show green because of Alexa 488 conjugated to an antibody against beta-III tubulin.
source: In this preparation, the blue fluorescence is of nuclei stained for DNA with DAPI, neurones show green because of Alexa 488 conjugated to an antibody against beta-III tubulin and astrocytes are red because of Alexa 546 conjugated to anti-GFAP (glial fibrillary acid protein).
evidence: This describes the staining protocol used.

claim: In the rat brain preparation, astrocytes are red because of Alexa 546 conjugated to anti-GFAP.
source: In this preparation, the blue fluorescence is of nuclei stained for DNA with DAPI, neurones show green because of Alexa 488 conjugated to an antibody against beta-III tubulin and astrocytes are red because of Alexa 546 conjugated to anti-GFAP (glial fibrillary acid protein).
evidence: This describes the staining protocol used.

claim: The rat brain image demonstrates the excellent chromatic correction of the lens with all three colours simultaneously in focus.
source: This image clearly shows the excellent chromatic correction of the lens with all three colours simultaneously in focus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-color image in Figure 3.

claim: The rat brain image demonstrates the possibility to view both the full large FOV and tiny details in the same image, using only software zoom.
source: Furthermore, the image demonstrates the possibility to view both the full large FOV and tiny details in the same image, using only (17x) software zoom.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: The same fixed, cleared and acridine orange-stained 10 day old mouse embryo was imaged with the Mesolens and with a dry objective lens of similar magnification (5x/0.15 N.A. HCX PL Fluotar, Leica Microsystems) to demonstrate superior sectioning capability.
source: To demonstrate the superior sectioning capability of the Mesolens compared to a standard objective lens with comparable magnification, we imaged the same fixed, cleared and acridine orange-stained 10 day old mouse embryo with the Mesolens and with a dry objective lens of similar magnification (5x/0.15 N.A. HCX PL Fluotar, Leica Microsystems) mounted on an upright laser scanning microscope.
evidence: This describes the comparison experiment.

claim: The Mesolens can image throughout the entire 2 mm thick embryo with sub-cellular resolution.
source: The Mesolens can image throughout the entire 2 mm thick embryo with sub-cellular resolution (we can see individual nuclei all the way through).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figure 4.

claim: Individual nuclei can be seen all the way through the 2 mm thick embryo with the Mesolens.
source: The Mesolens can image throughout the entire 2 mm thick embryo with sub-cellular resolution (we can see individual nuclei all the way through).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figure 4.

claim: The image with the commercial low magnification, low N.A. objective shows long needle-like vertical structures indicating very poor z resolution.
source: This is in contrast to the image with the commercial low magnification, low N.A. objective, where the long needle-like vertical structures indicate a very poor z resolution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison in Figure 4a.

claim: The lateral resolution remains micron-sized throughout the embryo with the Mesolens.
source: The lateral resolution also remains micron-sized throughout the embryo, as can been seen from Figure 4c, which presents an XY cross section midway through the same embryo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 4c.

claim: The dark cavity within the midbrain and the neural canal within the spinal cord are imaged with good axial resolution even though they are deep within the embryo.
source: In Figure 4b the dark cavity within the midbrain on the left and the neural canal within the spinal cord on the right are imaged with good axial resolution even though they are deep within the embryo, which is equally-well resolved at the top and bottom of the z range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 4b.

claim: Fine details such as the dark extracellular spaces in the neural tube and the epithelial cell monolayer are only visible in the Mesolens image.
source: Although the larger cavities are also visible in the image taken with the 5x lens, finer details such as the dark extracellular spaces in the bright neural tube to the right of the image and the epithelial cell monolayer (upper right margin and left lower corner) are only visible in the Mesolens image (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Individual cell nuclei in all the tissues are clearly resolved in the XY section.
source: In the XY section (Figure 4c) similar fine details including individual cell nuclei in all the tissues are clearly resolved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 4c.

claim: Structures within the embryo were identified by means of Kaufman, 1992.
source: Structures within the embryo were identified by means of (Kaufman, 1992).
evidence: This describes the method for anatomical identification and is supported by a citation.

claim: The constant signal with increasing depth throughout the specimen arises from having a well-cleared specimen.
source: The constant signal with increasing depth throughout the specimen arises from having a well-cleared specimen.
evidence: This is the authors' explanation for the observed signal uniformity.

claim: The laser power or detector gain was not adjusted when imaging deeper into tissue.
source: We did not adjust the laser power or detector gain when imaging deeper into tissue.
evidence: This describes the imaging protocol used.

claim: A 12.5 day old embryo was stained with an antibody against axonal beta tubulin coupled to Alexa 594 to highlight nerve cells.
source: This embryo was stained with an antibody against axonal beta tubulin coupled to the fluorescent dye Alexa 594, to highlight nerve cells and with acridine orange, here used chiefly as a nuclear marker.
evidence: This describes the staining protocol used.

claim: A 12.5 day old embryo was stained with acridine orange, used chiefly as a nuclear marker.
source: This embryo was stained with an antibody against axonal beta tubulin coupled to the fluorescent dye Alexa 594, to highlight nerve cells and with acridine orange, here used chiefly as a nuclear marker.
evidence: This describes the staining protocol used.

claim: In the 3D rendering there are 60 images axially separated by 3.33 µm, imaging a total thickness of 200 µm.
source: In the 3D rendering there are 60 images axially separated by 3.33 µm, imaging a total thickness of 200 µm and we used the fluorescence mode of our image reconstruction software (Volocity, Perkin Elmer) which applies a direct opacity rendering.
evidence: This describes the parameters of the 3D rendering in Video 2.

claim: Fine structures throughout the embryo such as the developing heart muscle fibers can be clearly identified.
source: We can clearly identify fine structures throughout the embryo such as the developing heart muscle fibers and fine details in the eye such as the corneal endothelium.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figure 5 and Video 2.

claim: Fine details in the eye such as the corneal endothelium can be clearly identified.
source: We can clearly identify fine structures throughout the embryo such as the developing heart muscle fibers and fine details in the eye such as the corneal endothelium.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figure 5 and Video 2.

claim: The inset in Figure 5 shows only a software zoom from the full scan range of the confocal Mesolens system, not a smaller scanned region.
source: We emphasize that this image is only a software zoom from the full scan range of the confocal Mesolens system, not a smaller scanned region.
evidence: This clarifies the nature of the zoomed image.

claim: In the eye, the lens was visible as a slightly absorbing structure with a sharply defined outline.
source: In the eye, the lens was visible as a slightly absorbing structure with a sharply defined outline, surrounded in turn by cells within the aqueous humour and then the strongly-stained retina.
evidence: This describes anatomical features visible in the images.

claim: All eye structures were enclosed in the corneal stroma, lined on the inside with the corneal endothelium and on the outside with the epithelial precursor of the conjunctiva.
source: All these structures were enclosed in the corneal stroma, lined on the inside with the corneal endothelium and on the outside with the epithelial precursor of the conjunctiva.
evidence: This describes anatomical features visible in the images.

claim: An outstanding axial resolution is retained over the full FOV with only a small degradation at the edges of the image.
source: To demonstrate that an outstanding axial resolution is retained over the full FOV with only a small degradation at the edges of the image we performed a two-color XZ image of the 12.5 day old embryo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is possible to design and construct an objective to facilitate imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of only a few microns.
source: We have shown here that it is possible, using known design software and fabrication to exact tolerances, to design and construct an objective to facilitate imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick in their entirety with depth resolution of only a few microns instead of the tens of microns currently attained, allowing sub-cellular detail to be resolved.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all the data presented.

claim: A design principle of more than a century is that the number of lateral resolution units in the field diameter should be approximately the same for all objectives.
source: In doing this work we have departed from a design principle of more than a century, which is that the number of lateral resolution units in the field diameter should be approximately the same for all objectives.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in microscope design.

claim: The lateral resolution in the image field of the Mesolens is too great for the human eye but suits cameras of the highest pixel number available or laser scanning confocal operation.
source: As we have shown here, the lateral resolution in the image field of this new lens is too great for the human eye, but suits cameras of the highest pixel number available or laser scanning confocal operation and, crucially, the axial resolution justifies the collection of several hundred optical sections of a thick specimen within the working depth.
evidence: This is based on the design specifications and imaging results.

claim: The axial resolution of the Mesolens justifies the collection of several hundred optical sections of a thick specimen within the working depth.
source: As we have shown here, the lateral resolution in the image field of this new lens is too great for the human eye, but suits cameras of the highest pixel number available or laser scanning confocal operation and, crucially, the axial resolution justifies the collection of several hundred optical sections of a thick specimen within the working depth.
evidence: This is based on the measured axial resolution and working distance.

claim: Single cells, including the nucleated erythrocytes of mouse embryos, and syncytial heart muscle fibres can be seen not just near the surface but throughout the depth of the embryo.
source: We have shown that single cells, including the nucleated erythrocytes of mouse embryos, and syncytial heart muscle fibres can be seen not just near the surface as with conventional objectives but throughout the depth of the embryo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: A biologist can discover whether a defect in development involves changes in the shape of a deep-located organ, or of cell shape or cell number, or of the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
source: A biologist can therefore discover whether, for example, a defect in development involves changes in the shape of a deep-located organ, or of cell shape or cell number, or of the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
evidence: This is inferred from the capabilities demonstrated by the Mesolens.

claim: No existing microscope can show all of these features simultaneously in an intact mouse embryo in a single image.
source: No existing microscope can show all of these features simultaneously in an intact mouse embryo in a single image.
evidence: This is stated as a unique capability of the Mesolens based on comparison with existing technologies.

claim: With the Mesolens there is the possibility of switching from a relatively slow laser scanning mode to fast camera mode with the large field of view in the same focal plane.
source: With the Mesolens we also have the possibility of switching from a relatively slow laser scanning mode to fast camera mode with the large field of view in the same focal plane.
evidence: This describes a capability of the Mesolens system.

claim: Switching between laser scanning and camera modes is not possible with higher magnification objective lenses.
source: This is not possible with higher magnification objective lenses.
evidence: This is based on the design limitations of high-magnification objectives.

claim: The ability to switch modes is of value both in searching for rare image features and in adjusting the compensation collars of the objective lens.
source: This is of value both in searching for rare image features, and in adjusting the compensation collars of the objective lens.
evidence: This is inferred from the practical advantages of the dual-mode capability.

claim: Difficulty with the penetration of the acridine orange stain might be part of the reason for the reduced signal in the centre of the 12.5 day old embryo.
source: We do not observe difficulty with the penetration of the acridine orange stain for the E10 embryos, although for the thicker 12.5 day old embryos this might be part of the reason for the reduced signal in the centre of the embryo seen in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed signal variation.

claim: The maximum size of a Mesolens dataset is approximately 200x that for a 100x/1.4 N.A. lens.
source: If the volume of the point spread function of an objective lens to the first ellipsoidal minimum is divided into the total accessible 3D volume a measure of the number of resolved voxels can be obtained (a quantity comparable to the Nyquist sample but for a 3D volume). The maximum size of a Mesolens dataset is approximately 200x that for a 100x/1.4 N.A. lens.
evidence: This is calculated from the PSF volumes and accessible volumes.

claim: A complete Mesolens image sampled at Nyquist resolution over the 6 mm x 6 mm x 3 mm volume generates a 639 GB digital image.
source: Calculated from the data presented here for the Mesolens, a complete image sampled at Nyquist resolution over the 6 mm x 6 mm x 3 mm volume generates a 639 GB digital image, which is large but the capacity and speed of current computers can readily handle data files of this size.
evidence: This is calculated from the volume and sampling requirements.

claim: The capacity and speed of current computers can readily handle data files of 639 GB.
source: Calculated from the data presented here for the Mesolens, a complete image sampled at Nyquist resolution over the 6 mm x 6 mm x 3 mm volume generates a 639 GB digital image, which is large but the capacity and speed of current computers can readily handle data files of this size.
evidence: This is stated as a known capability of current computing technology.

claim: The ability to record such high-volume data makes it likely that many applications other than the imaging of mouse embryos will be found.
source: The ability to record such high-volume data makes it likely that many applications other than the imaging of mouse embryos will be found.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications.

claim: Provided the problem of tissue transparency can be solved, there are obvious applications in neurobiology.
source: Provided the problem of tissue transparency can be solved, there are obvious applications in neurobiology.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications.

claim: The Mesolens can reveal spatially rare events and may have application in the measurement of the mitotic index in slowly-reproducing tissues.
source: Also, the Mesolens can reveal spatially rare events, and may have application in the measurement of the mitotic index in slowly-reproducing tissues.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the large FOV capability.

claim: The 25x higher optical throughput could facilitate imaging of weakly emitting specimens.
source: The 25x higher optical throughput could also facilitate imaging of weakly emitting specimens, for example specimens expressing fluorescent proteins at a low level or containing single cells bearing luciferase as a bioluminescent marker.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the measured throughput advantage.

claim: A lens of similar numerical aperture to the Mesolens (N.A.=0.6) with a field of 5 mm diameter and a collection depth of 1 mm has been described by Sofroniew et al., 2016.
source: Recently, a lens of similar numerical aperture to the Mesolens (N.A.=0.6) with a field of 5 mm diameter and a collection depth of 1 mm has been described (Sofroniew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sofroniew et al., 2016.

claim: The lens described by Sofroniew et al. is corrected only for a narrow wavelength band (900-1070 nm) and is restricted in use to single-spot multi-photon imaging.
source: However, this lens is corrected only for a narrow wavelength band (900–1070 nm) and is restricted in use to single-spot multi-photon imaging, whereas the Mesolens can serve as a multi-wavelength camera lens, a confocal objective, and potentially also as a multi-photon objective, both single-spot and wide-field (Amor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the cited specifications and comparison with the Mesolens.

claim: The Mesolens can serve as a multi-wavelength camera lens, a confocal objective, and potentially also as a multi-photon objective, both single-spot and wide-field.
source: However, this lens is corrected only for a narrow wavelength band (900–1070 nm) and is restricted in use to single-spot multi-photon imaging, whereas the Mesolens can serve as a multi-wavelength camera lens, a confocal objective, and potentially also as a multi-photon objective, both single-spot and wide-field (Amor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated capabilities and a citation to Amor et al., 2016.

claim: This development represents the most radical change in microscope objective design for over a century.
source: This development represents the most radical change in microscope objective design for over a century, and we believe that despite the fact that the Mesolens cannot be fitted to a conventional microscope stand, it has the potential to transform optical microscopy through the acquisition of sub-cellular resolution 3D datasets from large tissue specimens.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the significance of their work.

claim: The Mesolens has the potential to transform optical microscopy through the acquisition of sub-cellular resolution 3D datasets from large tissue specimens.
source: This development represents the most radical change in microscope objective design for over a century, and we believe that despite the fact that the Mesolens cannot be fitted to a conventional microscope stand, it has the potential to transform optical microscopy through the acquisition of sub-cellular resolution 3D datasets from large tissue specimens.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the potential impact based on the demonstrated capabilities.
